cloud.title: Cloud Fundamental
cloud.deck: Platform names change. The parts do not: a place to run, a place to store, a network, an identity, and a bill. These notes stay on that shared model.

sections.label: The cloud model
sections.html:
The cloud model

A cloud provider runs large pools of machines, disks, and networks, and rents slices of them through an API. You stop ordering hardware for each new service. You start describing what you want, and you pay for what stays switched on.

Elasticity is the ability to add or remove capacity. Scalability is the ability of the design to handle growth at all. A single large virtual machine can be scaled up until it cannot. An elastic design adds copies and later removes them.

How much of the stack you still operate.
ModelYou manageProvider manages
Infrastructure as a serviceOperating system, runtime, application, dataHardware, hypervisor, the physical network
Platform as a serviceApplication and dataRuntime patching, the machines underneath
Software as a serviceConfiguration, users, and the data you uploadThe application itself

Places

A region is a group of data centers in a geography. An availability zone is an isolated group inside that region, with separate power and network. Putting two copies in one zone protects you from a bad deploy. Putting them in two zones protects you from a building. Putting them in two regions protects you from a region, and it costs more in latency, data transfer, and operational work.

The account, subscription, or project is the blast-radius boundary. Production and experiments should not share one. Bills, permissions, and quotas attach to that boundary.

sections.label: Compute
sections.html:
Compute

Compute is anything that runs your code. The useful split is how long it lives and what you must patch.

  • Virtual machines look like servers. You choose the size, the image, and usually the operating system patches. They fit long-running processes, licensed software, and lift-and-shift.
  • Containers package a process and its dependencies. You still need something to run the containers: a service, or a cluster you operate. They fit when many services should share the same deployment shape.
  • Functions run for one event or request, then disappear. The provider patches the runtime. They fit irregular traffic and glue between services. They fit poorly when you need a long-held connection, local disk, or a cold start that breaks the latency budget.

Stateless compute is easier to scale. Put durable data in a store, not on the instance disk. An instance can disappear in a replacement, a scale-in, or a zone failure. If the only copy of a file lived there, it is gone.

Scale out by adding copies when the work can be split. Scale up by buying a bigger machine when the work cannot. Most "just make it bigger" stories end when the biggest size is still not enough.

sections.label: Storage
sections.html:
Storage

Pick storage from the access pattern, not from the product name.

Three shapes, three jobs.
ShapeLooks likeGood for
BlockA disk attached to a machineDatabases and anything that expects a filesystem on one host
FileA shared filesystemSeveral machines reading the same tree
ObjectA key and a blob, reached over HTTPUploads, backups, images, data files, static sites

Object storage is durable because the provider keeps copies. It is not a POSIX disk, and it is not a database. You do not edit a byte in the middle. You write a new object.

A managed database is someone else's operational work: patching, backups, and often failover. You still own schema, indexes, query shape, and the decision about what the data means. Running the database yourself is reasonable when you need a specific version, extension, or placement. It is an ongoing job, not a checkbox.

Copies

Durability is "the provider did not lose the bits." Availability is "you can read them now." A backup is a separate copy you can restore, preferably in another region, with a tested restore. A replica that accepts the same bad write as the primary is not a backup.

sections.label: Networking
sections.html:
Networking

A virtual network is your address space inside the provider. Subnets divide it. Routes and security rules decide what may talk. Private subnets have no direct route from the internet. Public ones do, and that should be a small set: load balancers and bastions, not every application server.

  • Load balancer. Spreads traffic across healthy copies and gives callers one address. Health checks must match real readiness, or the balancer will send users to a process that is up and useless.
  • DNS. Turns names into addresses. Use it for failover only when you have measured how long caches keep the old answer.
  • TLS. Protects the hop you terminate. Termination at the load balancer is common. Traffic behind it should still be restricted, and sometimes encrypted again, depending on who else shares the network.

Egress is easy to forget in the design and obvious on the bill. Data leaving a region, or leaving the provider toward the internet, is often priced differently from data staying inside. A chatty service that pulls from another region on every request will show up as cost before it shows up as latency you noticed.

Draw trust boundaries first: internet, your network, the data store, the management plane. Then place controls on the lines you actually cross.

sections.label: Identity and access
sections.html:
Identity and access

Every call is made by someone or something. Users are people. Workloads are the programs: a virtual machine, a function, a pipeline. They should not share an account. A person leaving the team is not the same event as rotating what a service uses.

  • Grant the smallest permission that lets the job finish. Wide roles feel faster until a leaked key can do everything the admin can do.
  • Prefer short-lived credentials issued to the workload. Long-lived keys in a repository or a laptop are a common breach path.
  • Federate human login to one identity provider so joiners and leavers are handled in one place.
  • Separate the permission to change infrastructure from the permission to read production data.

Audit logs answer "who did what." Turn them on before you need them, and send them somewhere the same account cannot quietly delete. A trail that the attacker can erase is a diary, not evidence.

Identity is the real perimeter. Network rules still matter, but a valid key from anywhere will walk past a diagram that only shows firewalls.

sections.label: Cost and responsibility
sections.html:
Cost and responsibility

The shared responsibility model is the contract under the marketing. The provider secures the cloud: buildings, hardware, the hypervisor. You secure what you put in it: accounts, data, network exposure, and most configuration. On infrastructure as a service you patch the guest operating system. On functions the provider patches the platform, and you still own the code and the permissions it runs with.

Where money goes

  • Compute that is on while idle. Stop it, or size it to the real load.
  • Storage you forgot: old snapshots, unused disks, logs with no expiry.
  • Data transfer across regions and out to the internet.
  • Over-provisioned managed services left at their default size.

Tag resources with the system and the environment so a bill can be read. Set a budget alert before the month closes. A quota protects the account from a runaway loop. A budget alert tells a person.

Deleting an experiment is part of the design. If you cannot say who owns a resource, you cannot say whether it should still be running.

kubernetes.title: Kubernetes
kubernetes.deck: Kubernetes keeps a cluster moving toward the state you declared. These notes cover the objects you actually write, and the habits that make a cluster operable.

sections.label: The cluster picture
sections.html:
The cluster picture

A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane and a set of worker nodes. You submit a desired state, usually as YAML: "three copies of this container, reachable under this name." Controllers watch the current state and try to close the gap. That loop is the product. SSH into a node is a debugging tool, not the way you make a change stick.

The API server is the front door. etcd stores the cluster data. Schedulers place pods onto nodes that have room. Kubelets on each node start the containers the scheduler assigned. You can run this yourself, or you can use a managed control plane and still own the workloads, the identity, and the network policy.

If a change is not in the manifest that Git holds, the next reconcile can erase it. The cluster is a mirror. The repository is the source.

Labels are the join key

Kubernetes does not wire objects by memory address. A Service selects pods by labels. A network rule selects pods by labels. Spend the time to make labels boring and consistent: application, component, environment. A typo in a selector looks like "the app is down" when the app is running and invisible.

sections.label: Pods
sections.html:
Pods

A pod is the smallest thing you deploy. It is one or more containers that share a network namespace, which means they share localhost, and they can share volumes. Containers in a pod are started, scheduled, and die together. Most pods hold one application container. A second container is justified when it must share the pod's files or network: a proxy sidecar, or a helper that refreshes a certificate into a shared volume.

Pods are ephemeral. The disk inside the container goes away with the pod unless you mounted a volume. The pod IP changes when the pod is replaced. Callers should use a Service name, not a pod IP they happened to see.

Probes

  • Startup tells the kubelet the process is still booting, so a slow start is not mistaken for a deadlock.
  • Readiness tells the Service whether this pod should receive traffic. Fail it when a dependency you need is down.
  • Liveness restarts the container. Use it for a stuck process. Do not use it for a downed database, or the cluster will restart healthy code in a loop.

Requests and limits

A CPU or memory request is what the scheduler reserves. A limit is what the container is allowed to use. Without requests, the scheduler can pack a node until everything is slow. A memory limit that is too low kills the process. Set requests from a measurement, not from a guess you copy between services.

sections.label: Workloads
sections.html:
Workloads

You rarely create pods by hand. A workload controller creates them and replaces them when they disappear.

Choose the controller from identity and lifetime, not from habit.
ControllerUse when
DeploymentYou want N interchangeable copies. A rolling update replaces them. This is the default for stateless HTTP services.
StatefulSetEach replica needs a stable name, ordered startup, or its own disk. Databases and queues often land here, and they still need care that a YAML file does not supply.
DaemonSetEvery node (or a selected set) should run one copy: log collectors, network agents.
JobThe work should run to completion, then stop.
CronJobThe work should run on a schedule. Make the task safe to run twice, because a retry will.

A Deployment owns a ReplicaSet, which owns the pods. Roll back the Deployment, not a single pod. Deleting a pod is a restart. It is not a rollback, and it is not a fix for a bad image.

Horizontal scaling adds pods. It only helps when one request does not need more resources than a single pod has, and when sessions are not trapped on one copy.

sections.label: Services and traffic
sections.html:
Services and traffic

Every pod can reach every other pod by IP, across nodes. That flat network is convenient and it is also a wide default. Treat it as a starting point, then restrict it when the cluster holds more than one trust level.

A Service gives a stable name to a changing set of pods.
TypeWho can use it
ClusterIPOther workloads inside the cluster. This is the normal choice.
NodePortA port on every node. Useful for demos and odd network setups, noisy as a public design.
LoadBalancerAn external load balancer from the platform, with its own address.

HTTP routing sits above Services. An Ingress, or a Gateway, maps host names and paths to Services and often terminates TLS. The controller behind that object is a separate install. The Ingress resource does nothing until a controller is watching it.

Cluster DNS resolves Service names. Prefer name.namespace.svc.cluster.local in documentation, and the short name name only from callers in the same namespace. Cross-namespace calls should be explicit so a rename is visible.

NetworkPolicy is a lock you add once you know the allowed paths. An empty policy that selects nothing protects nothing. A policy that selects pods and lists no ingress denies them.

sections.label: Configuration
sections.html:
Configuration

Keep configuration out of the image. The same image should run in a test namespace and in production, with different config. Bake the build identity into the image. Inject the environment at deploy time.

  • ConfigMap holds plain settings: feature flags, addresses, small files. It is not secret, and it is not a place for a large binary.
  • Secret holds credentials and keys. The value is base64-encoded in the API, which is encoding, not encryption. Encryption at rest is a cluster setting. Anyone who can read Secrets in the namespace can use them.
  • Environment variables are easy and frozen at process start. Mounted files can be updated without a restart if the application re-reads them. Pick the one the process actually supports.

Do not store live Secrets in a public Git repository. A common pattern is to commit encrypted or referenced secrets, and let a controller materialize the Kubernetes Secret in the cluster. The manifest you review should not contain the raw password.

A ConfigMap change does not restart pods by itself. If the process only reads the environment at startup, roll the workload or the new value will sit unused.

sections.label: Day-2 operations
sections.html:
Day-2 operations

The first deploy is the easy day. The cluster earns its cost on the days a node disappears, a rollout sticks, or a namespace runs out of memory.

Rollouts

A rolling update starts new pods before, or as, it stops old ones, depending on the surge and unavailable settings. Readiness must go green only when the new pod can serve. If readiness is always true, the rollout will happily replace a working version with a broken one. Keep the previous ReplicaSet so rollback is a declared change, not a scavenger hunt.

Namespaces and quotas

A namespace is a folder for names and a boundary for policy. It is not a strong security boundary by itself, but it is where you attach resource quotas, default limits, and who may deploy. Production and development on one cluster should at least be separate namespaces, with separate permissions. Many teams use separate clusters once the blast radius matters more than the extra cost.

What to look at

  • Events and pod status explain scheduling and crash loops.
  • Logs explain the process. Ship them off the node, because the node will be replaced.
  • Metrics explain saturation: CPU throttling, memory approaching the limit, restart counts.
  • A request id that crosses services explains a single failure better than a dashboard of averages.
kubectl is a window onto the API. Changes made only there will drift. Prefer a pull request that changes the manifest, then watch the controllers catch up.

ai-ml.title: AI / ML
ai-ml.deck: A model is one step in a pipeline. These notes follow the path from a decision you need, through data and evaluation, to a system that can be turned off safely.

sections.label: Map of the work
sections.html:
Map of the work

Machine learning builds a function from examples instead of writing every rule by hand. Artificial intelligence is the broader aim: systems that take on tasks we associate with judgment. Most useful systems are narrower than the aim. They classify, rank, forecast, or generate, inside a boundary someone chose.

A model is that function plus its parameters. It is the middle of a pipeline:

  1. Decide the action the system may take, and the cost of being wrong.
  2. Collect examples that match the moment of decision, not a convenient export.
  3. Train, then measure against a baseline a person could explain.
  4. Serve the model behind the same standards as any other dependency: latency, failure, and a way to roll back.
  5. Watch the inputs. A model does not announce that the world moved.
If a short rule or a query already makes the decision well, a model is extra machinery. Start there. Add learning when the rule table is what keeps breaking.

sections.label: Kinds of learning
sections.html:
Kinds of learning

The kind of learning follows from the feedback you have, not from whichever algorithm is popular this year.

Match the setup to the signal you can actually collect.
SetupThe signalTypical job
SupervisedEach example has a label or a target numberSpam or not, price, next value, "which class"
UnsupervisedNo labels, only the structure in the inputsGrouping, finding odd points, compressing
ReinforcementA reward after a sequence of actionsControl and game-like decisions, expensive to get right outside a simulator

A discriminative model scores or labels an input. A generative model draws new samples that resemble its training data. Generation is not understanding, and a fluent paragraph is not a checked fact. If the product needs a source of truth, put retrieval or a system of record next to the model and design for the case where they disagree.

Transfer learning starts from a model trained on a broad set and adapts it to a smaller one. It helps when your labeled set is thin and the broad model has seen similar inputs. It still needs an evaluation on your data. A leaderboard score is not that evaluation.

sections.label: Data and features
sections.html:
Data and features

Label quality beats model cleverness more often than notes like this admit. A clean definition of the label, written down, is part of the system. "Churn" that means three different things to three teams will train a model that is sure and useless.

Leakage

Leakage is when the training rows contain information that will not exist at decision time, or information that is the answer in disguise. A column copied from the outcome, a feature computed with the full future window, or a random split that puts the same user in both train and test: the offline score looks wonderful, and production looks ordinary.

Splits

  • Split by time when the world moves forward. Train on the past, test on a later period.
  • Split by entity when rows are repeated per user, device, or account, so the model cannot memorize an identity.
  • Random row splits are for independent rows. Most business tables are not independent rows.

A feature must be computable when you predict. If building it requires tomorrow's table, it is not a feature. It is a leak, or it is a batch job you have not scheduled. Document the freshness: how old the value may be, and what the model should do when it is missing.

Bias in the collection shows up as confidence later. Who is missing from the examples will be the group the metric does not describe.

sections.label: Training and evaluation
sections.html:
Training and evaluation

Training fits parameters to a training set. Evaluation asks whether the fit helps on data the fit did not see. Report the second number. Keep a baseline next to it: the majority class, the current rule, or a small linear model. A complex model that does not beat the baseline has not earned its operational cost.

Metrics follow the cost of errors

  • Accuracy hides failure when one class is rare. A model that always says "no fraud" can be 99% accurate and never catch a case.
  • Precision is the share of alarms that were right. Low precision trains people to ignore the system.
  • Recall is the share of real cases you caught. Low recall is silent miss.
  • Calibration asks whether a score of 0.8 is right about four times in five. Rankings can look fine while the probability is fiction. Do not show an uncalibrated score as a probability.

Slice the metric. An average can rise while a region, a language, or a customer tier gets worse. The slice you refuse to measure is the one that will page you.

Offline evaluation is a filter, not a launch. When the cost of a wrong action is high, shadow the model on live traffic, or send a small share of decisions, before it acts alone. Watch the decision, not only the loss curve.

sections.label: Serving
sections.html:
Serving

A trained file is not a service. Serving is an ordinary production problem with a versioned artifact in the middle.

  • Batch scores a table on a schedule. It fits when the decision can wait: nightly limits, morning lists.
  • Online scores one request inside a latency budget. It needs a feature lookup that is as fast as the model, and a timeout.
  • Fallback is the path when the model is slow, down, or unsure. A default rule, a previous score, or a human queue. Shipping without a fallback is shipping a hard dependency.

Version the model, the code that builds features, and the training data pointer together. A rollback that restores the model and leaves a new feature definition in place is not a rollback. Record the version on each prediction so a bad week can be traced.

After launch

Input drift means today's examples do not look like training. Prediction drift means the score distribution moved. Neither proves the decisions got worse, and a stable dashboard does not prove they stayed good. Keep a sample of outcomes, with a delay that matches how long the truth takes to arrive, and compare.

Cache a prediction only when the same inputs must yield the same action. Do not cache your way past a user who withdrew consent or a price that changed.

sections.label: Judgment and limits
sections.html:
Judgment and limits

A model repeats patterns in the data, including unfair ones and outdated ones. It does not know your policy. Policy has to be written beside it: who may be scored, what the score may change, and which decisions stay with a person.

  • State the intended use and the uses that are out of scope. A model fit for ranking search results is not a model fit for denying a service.
  • Treat training data as data you are accountable for. Private text, customer records, and scraped content do not become harmless because a training job consumed them.
  • Generated text can be confident and false. If you display it, give the reader a way to see the source, or do not present it as a record.
  • Keep a person responsible for the decision the system informs. "The model said so" is not an owner.
  • Plan to turn the model off. If the business cannot run the fallback for a day, you do not have a model in the loop. You have a single point of failure with a research name.
Measure harm on the groups affected, not only on the average user. A small overall error can still be a large error for the people with the least room to absorb it.

microservices.title: Microservices
microservices.deck: A microservice is a deployable boundary with its own data and its own reason to change. These notes stay on that boundary, not on a diagram full of boxes.

sections.label: The boundary
sections.html:
The boundary

Split a system where the business already splits. Orders, catalog, and billing change for different reasons and are often owned by different people. That is a candidate boundary. A function that is merely "small" is not.

Each service should be deployable without a lockstep release of the others. If every change still needs three teams to ship on the same day, the split is only a network hop.

Start with a modular codebase and a clear data owner. Extract a service when independent deploy is the pain you are relieving.

sections.label: Owned data
sections.html:
Owned data

A service owns the tables it writes. Other services ask it, or subscribe to what it publishes. They do not share its database. A shared database hides the coupling until a column rename takes the neighbors down.

  • One writer for each fact.
  • Copies elsewhere are caches or projections, with a known delay.
  • A transaction that must update two services is a design smell. Put the rule in one service, or accept a process that can be retried.

sections.label: Contracts
sections.html:
Contracts

The contract is the request, the response, and the errors a caller can handle. Write it down. A breaking change is a new version, or a field that callers can ignore until they are ready.

Do not leak your tables through the API. Return the words the caller needs. Internal names can change without a coordinated release.

sections.label: Calls between services
sections.html:
Calls between services

A synchronous call is simple and it couples availability. If the catalog is down, checkout waits. Use it when the caller cannot continue without the answer and the latency budget allows it.

An event is better when the receiver can act later. The publisher records that something happened. Consumers react, and they must tolerate duplicates and uncertain order. Name the event for the fact, not for the command you wish the other team would run.

sections.label: Failure
sections.html:
Failure

The network will drop calls, and a dependency will be slow. Time out. Limit how many calls you pile up. Decide the fallback: a cached answer, a smaller feature, or a clear error. Retry only when the operation is safe to run twice.

Give every request an id that crosses services. A dashboard of averages will not tell you which checkout failed.

devops.title: DevOps
devops.deck: DevOps is the habit of shipping a small change and knowing, quickly, whether it helped. These notes follow that loop from source to the running system.

sections.label: The loop
sections.html:
The loop

A change is not done when the code is merged. It is done when it is running, observed, and reversible. The same people who write the change should be able to see it fail and roll it back.

Small batches make that possible. A release that contains a month of work hides the cause. A release that contains one change tells you where to look.

sections.label: Build
sections.html:
Build

The build should be repeatable. Same source, same result. Pin the dependencies. Do not compile on a laptop and copy the artifact by hand.

  • One artifact, promoted through environments. Do not rebuild with different flags for production.
  • Tests that must pass before the artifact exists: unit checks, and a small set of contract checks.
  • A version you can point at: a commit id on the artifact and in the running process.

sections.label: Pipeline
sections.html:
Pipeline

The pipeline is the only path to production. If someone can still shell in and patch a server, the pipeline is a suggestion. Steps should be visible: build, test, publish, deploy, and a check that the new version is serving.

A green pipeline that never looks at the running system will ship a process that starts and then fails its first request.

sections.label: Environments
sections.html:
Environments

Development, a shared test environment, and production should differ by configuration, not by a mystery set of manual steps. Secrets stay out of the repository. Data in test is either synthetic or carefully reduced. Production data does not travel to a laptop.

Name who is allowed to deploy where. Production is a smaller group, and the action is still a recorded change, not a private click.

sections.label: After release
sections.html:
After release

Watch the new version, not only the cluster. Error rate, latency, and a business signal such as completed checkouts. Keep the previous version ready so rollback is a deploy, not a reconstruction.

Write down what you learned when a release hurts. The next pipeline check should catch that class of mistake. An incident that only lives in chat will happen again.

case-study.title: Case Study
case-study.deck: A case study is useful when it shows the constraint, not only the architecture diagram. These notes are a way to read one, and a place to file the next one.

sections.label: How to read one
sections.html:
How to read one

Start with the question the system had to answer, and the limit it could not ignore: latency, cost, a regulation, a team size, a traffic spike. The boxes on the diagram are the answer to that limit. Without the limit, the diagram is fashion.

Add a new case here as its own subsection when you have those facts. A title, the constraint, the design, and the outcome are enough. A slide full of product names is not.

sections.label: Constraint
sections.html:
Constraint

Write the constraint in one sentence. "Checkout must answer in under 200 milliseconds." "Two teams must deploy without waiting for each other." "The audit trail cannot be edited." If you cannot say it, you cannot judge the design.

Also write what was deliberately left out. A system that ignores search, or ignores multi-region, is not incomplete if that was the deal. It is incomplete if readers are not told.

sections.label: Design
sections.html:
Design

Name the few parts that carry the constraint. A cache in front of a catalog. A queue between payment and fulfillment. A single service that owns the ledger. Resist listing every sidecar.

  • What data is the source of truth.
  • What is allowed to be stale.
  • How a request is identified from the edge to the store.

sections.label: What broke
sections.html:
What broke

Every honest case has a failure. A cache that served a price after it changed. A queue that grew until orders were hours late. A rollout that passed health checks and still dropped payments. Record the symptom, the cause, and the change that followed.

A case with no failure mode is an advertisement. Treat it as incomplete.

sections.label: What to copy
sections.html:
What to copy

Copy the decision, not the vendor list. If your constraint matches, the shape may match. If your traffic, team, or data rules do not, leave the shape alone. Write one line: "Use this when…" and "Do not use this when…".

File the next study as a new section in this page. Link it from the left navigation, keep the same four questions, and push the page. The home card already points here.

learning-path.title: Learning Path
learning-path.deck: Read these notes in an order that builds a small system, not in the order the cards happen to sit on the home page.

sections.label: Suggested order
sections.html:
Suggested order

Do not try to finish every page before you build anything. One pass through the vocabulary, one small design, then the notes that explain how that design is shipped and how it fails.

  1. Cloud Fundamental, so the words for place, compute, storage, and identity are shared.
  2. Architect Design Patterns, so a local mess and a system-wide style are not confused.
  3. Microservices, only after you can say what must deploy apart.
  4. Kubernetes and DevOps, so the design can be run and changed.
  5. Case Study, to test the design against someone else's constraint.
  6. AI / ML, when a model is actually part of the decision, not as a first step.

sections.label: Vocabulary
sections.html:
Vocabulary

Spend the first pass on names you will reuse: region, request and limit, service boundary, pipeline, readiness. If a term is fuzzy, stay on that section until you can explain it without the page open.

Skip ahead only when the current section is not the problem you have. A team already running a cluster does not need to pretend they have never seen a pod. They do need the failure notes.

sections.label: Shape a system
sections.html:
Shape a system

Pick one workflow you know, such as placing an order or publishing a document. Write the constraint, the data owner, and the one dependency that would hurt if it were slow. Then open the pattern and microservice notes and see which split you actually need.

A learning design that needs five services on day one is practicing diagrams. Two processes and a database will teach more.

sections.label: Run and change it
sections.html:
Run and change it

Put the small system somewhere you can deploy twice. Use the DevOps notes for the pipeline and the Kubernetes notes if the runtime is a cluster. Change one thing, watch one signal, and roll it back on purpose.

The point is the loop, not the platform logo. A single virtual machine with a repeatable deploy still counts.

sections.label: Go deeper
sections.html:
Go deeper

After the loop works, return to the section that felt thin. Add a subsection on that topic page rather than starting a second notebook. A case study belongs on the Case Study page, in the same four questions: constraint, design, what broke, what to copy.

When a new shelf is large enough for its own card, add the folder, link it from the home page, and push to main. The deploy workflow publishes the new tile.

system-design.title: System Design
system-design.deck: Beginner-friendly case studies. Each page has a blueprint of the internal modules, an explanation of what every module owns, and the core concepts that module uses.

sections.label: Twitter / X
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A social timeline looks simple: write a short post, then read a river of posts from people you follow. The hard part is the imbalance. Reads vastly outnumber writes, a few accounts have tens of millions of followers, and people expect a fresh feed in a few hundred milliseconds. The design therefore splits write work, read work, and search, and it treats celebrity fan-out as a special case.

System blueprint

The blueprint is a hybrid fan-out design. Ordinary posts are copied toward follower timelines at publish time. Very large accounts stay in a post store and are merged when someone opens the app. Search is a separate index, not a scan of the timeline cache.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. API gateway

Every mobile or web call lands here first. The gateway authenticates the session, applies per-user and per-IP limits, and routes writes to the tweet service and reads to timeline or search. It is also where you terminate TLS and attach a request ID. Keep this layer thin. If it starts composing timelines or talking to every store, one bad deploy can take the product down and you lose a clean place to shed load.

Core concepts in this module

  • Authentication
  • Rate limiting
  • Request routing
  • Load shedding

2. Tweet service

This is the source of truth for a post. It validates size and media, assigns a unique sortable ID, writes the post, and publishes an event. It does not walk millions of followers. That keeps the user-facing write fast and makes retries safe: the same client token should create one post, not two. Media binaries belong in object storage; this service stores only metadata and pointers.

Core concepts in this module

  • Write-ahead persistence
  • Unique IDs
  • Idempotent create
  • Event outbox

3. Fan-out workers

Workers consume the publish event and decide how to distribute it. For a typical account they push a lightweight reference into each follower's timeline cache. For an account with a huge audience they skip the copy and leave the post to be pulled later. This is the push-versus-pull decision. Workers must be able to pause, retry, and rebuild a slice of the graph without blocking the original writer.

Core concepts in this module

  • Timeline fan-out
  • Push vs pull
  • Backpressure
  • Partial rebuild

4. Timeline service

The home feed is a merge, not a dump of one list. The service reads cached entries for people you follow, adds recent posts from high-follower accounts, removes content you should not see, and pages with a cursor. Cursor pagination stays stable as new posts arrive; offset pagination does not. This module can be scaled by user shard because one person's feed does not need another person's cache.

Core concepts in this module

  • Read-time merge
  • Cursor pagination
  • Visibility filtering
  • User sharding

5. Search service

Search is a different product from the home feed. It needs an inverted index of terms, hashtags, and sometimes users. Indexing is asynchronous so a publish stays fast. Queries are served from replicas close to the reader. Do not reuse the timeline cache as a search engine; it is ordered by follow graph and time, not by term.

Core concepts in this module

  • Inverted index
  • Async indexing
  • Replica reads
  • Query ranking

6. Post store, follow graph, and caches

The post store keeps durable posts. The follow graph answers who should receive or see a post. The timeline cache makes the common home-feed read cheap. The search index makes term lookup cheap. Each store has a different consistency need: a missing cache entry is recoverable, a missing post write is not, and a stale follow edge can leak or hide content. Design expiry, rebuild, and authorization around those differences.

Core concepts in this module

  • Source of truth vs cache
  • Graph lookups
  • Cache invalidation
  • Hot-key handling

How the modules work together

A publish request is authenticated at the gateway, stored by the tweet service, and emitted as an event. Fan-out workers read the follow graph and write compact entries into timeline caches for ordinary followers. A home-timeline request asks the timeline service for those cached IDs, merges recent posts from a small celebrity set, filters deleted or muted content, and returns a cursor. Search never walks the cache; it queries its own inverted index. If a cache is missing, the timeline can be rebuilt from the post store and follow graph.

sections.label: YouTube
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Video is a two-sided system: creators upload large files that must be processed, and viewers stream those files from a nearby edge with changing network quality. The upload cannot live inside a single application server, and the playback path cannot depend on a long chain of business services. The blueprint therefore splits an asynchronous media pipeline from a cacheable playback path.

System blueprint

Original bytes are immutable. Derived renditions are produced by workers and published only when complete. The player never downloads one giant file; it reads a manifest and small segments.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Upload session

Large files fail if you ask the browser to POST once. A session issues an upload ID, accepts chunks, records offsets, and lets the client resume. Integrity checks belong here so a retry does not create a second video. When the last chunk arrives, this module writes a completion event instead of transcoding inline. That keeps user-facing latency predictable and isolates a slow encoder from the upload API.

Core concepts in this module

  • Resumable upload
  • Chunk checksums
  • Idempotent commit
  • Direct-to-storage

2. Transcoder farm

Raw uploads are the wrong shape for phones, TVs, and poor networks. Workers read the original, produce several resolutions and codecs, package segments, and write a manifest. Jobs are pulled from a durable queue so a crashed worker does not lose the video. Outputs should be written to new keys and published atomically. Never overwrite the original; it is the only way to retry or re-encode later.

Core concepts in this module

  • Transcoding
  • Job queues
  • Immutable outputs
  • Atomic publish

3. Catalog

The catalog is the product database: title, owner, visibility, processing state, and pointers to manifests. It is not the video file. Viewers and search read this metadata. A video that is still processing must not appear as ready. Privacy and takedown checks belong here so a CDN URL is not enough to watch a private upload.

Core concepts in this module

  • Metadata vs blob
  • State machine
  • Authorization
  • Eventual listing

4. Playback service and CDN

Playback should be a short control-plane call plus a data-plane fetch. The service authorizes the viewer and returns a manifest location, often with a signed URL. The CDN holds popular segments near the user. Adaptive bitrate is a player behavior: it measures buffer and bandwidth, then picks the next segment. If catalog or recommendations are down, an already authorized stream should still play.

Core concepts in this module

  • Signed URLs
  • CDN caching
  • Adaptive bitrate
  • Control vs data plane

5. Object storage, metadata, and jobs

Object storage keeps originals and renditions. The metadata database keeps product state. The job queue keeps work that may take minutes. These three fail differently: storage needs durability and lifecycle rules, metadata needs transactional state changes, and the queue needs retries without duplicate published videos. A consistent naming scheme for object keys makes cleanup and republish possible.

Core concepts in this module

  • Object immutability
  • Lifecycle policies
  • At-least-once jobs
  • Key design

How the modules work together

A creator starts a resumable upload session, sends chunks to object storage, and commits. The catalog records a processing video and a worker queue receives a job. Transcoders produce renditions and a manifest. Only then does the catalog mark the video playable. A viewer asks the playback service for an authorized manifest URL; the player fetches segments from the CDN and switches bitrate as the buffer changes. Failed transcodes retry from the original object, not from a half-written output.

sections.label: Netflix
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Streaming a movie is mostly moving large, cacheable files to a living room. Choosing the title, personalizing the home screen, and authorizing the device are different problems. Netflix-style designs isolate those control-plane services and push bytes to an Open Connect-like CDN so a recommendation outage does not stop playback.

System blueprint

Microservices are useful when they keep the playback path short. The important architectural choice is which calls are allowed to sit on the path of the next video segment.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Open Connect CDN

This is the data plane. Popular titles are pre-positioned on appliances or caches close to ISPs. The player downloads short segments. Because the files are immutable renditions, caches are simple and cheap. The design goal is that a Saturday-night hit never travels from a single origin to every household. Capacity planning here is about fill, eviction, and peering, not about adding more application servers.

Core concepts in this module

  • Edge caching
  • Content pre-positioning
  • Immutable segments
  • Origin shielding

2. Playback API and auth

Before bytes move, the device must be allowed to watch this title on this account. The playback API issues a short-lived license or token, chooses a CDN set, and records the session. It should not stream the movie itself. Keeping authorization in one place lets you revoke a device, enforce concurrency limits, and change CDN routing without touching every microservice.

Core concepts in this module

  • Short-lived licenses
  • Device limits
  • Session records
  • Token expiry

3. Identity, catalog, and recommendations

These services make the product feel personal, but they have different availability needs. Identity must work to start a session. Catalog can serve a slightly stale title list. Recommendations can fail open to a default row. Treating them as independent microservices is useful only if the client has fallbacks. A chain of synchronous calls from the home screen to every personalization model is the opposite of resilience.

Core concepts in this module

  • Microservices
  • Fallback UX
  • Stale-OK reads
  • Bulkheads

4. Viewing events and origin

Playback telemetry is valuable and dangerous. It should never block the next segment. Events go to a stream for quality metrics, recommendations, and billing. Origin storage holds the source files used to fill caches. The origin is expensive and far away, so only cache misses and new publishes should hit it. Separate the analytics pipeline from the path that keeps the picture moving.

Core concepts in this module

  • Async telemetry
  • Event streams
  • Cache fill
  • Failure isolation

How the modules work together

The client asks identity and playback auth for a license and nearby CDN hosts. Catalog and recommendations help the user choose a title, but once playback starts the player mostly talks to the CDN. Viewing events stream off to the side for ranking and billing. If recommendations fail, the app can show a smaller cached row. If a CDN node is overloaded, the client tries another host. Origin storage is a fallback, not the default path for a popular title.

sections.label: Uber
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Ride matching is a real-time marketplace. Riders want a car now, drivers move continuously, and the system must assign one driver to one trip even when two requests arrive together. The design splits fast-changing location data from durable trip state, then treats dispatch as a serialized decision.

System blueprint

H3-like cells turn a map into buckets you can query. ETA is an estimate built from routing and recent traffic, not a promise stored as truth.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Location ingest

Phones send frequent, noisy GPS points. This module validates, smooths, and writes the latest point into a cell-based index. It should not open a database transaction for every ping. Old points expire so a driver who went offline disappears from search. Because drivers cross city boundaries, the ingest path must handle partition moves without creating two live locations for one vehicle.

Core concepts in this module

  • Geospatial indexing
  • TTL locations
  • Noisy GPS
  • Hot city cells

2. Dispatch

Dispatch is the matcher. It searches nearby cells, applies product rules such as car type or rating, and proposes a driver. Two dispatchers can see the same idle driver, so the assignment must be fenced: a lease, a version number, or a unique active-trip constraint. Dispatch can retry with a larger radius, but it must never leave two confirmed trips on one driver.

Core concepts in this module

  • Matching
  • Leases / fencing
  • Idempotent assign
  • Search radius

3. ETA and routing

ETA combines map distance, live traffic, and pickup walking time. It is used to rank candidates and to set expectations, not to lock a car. Because routing is expensive, dispatch should ask it only for a shortlist. A degraded ETA service should fall back to straight-line time rather than block matching entirely.

Core concepts in this module

  • Routing graphs
  • Traffic signals
  • Approximate ETA
  • Degraded fallback

4. Trip service and trip store

The trip is a state machine: requested, assigned, arriving, in progress, completed, canceled. Payments, receipts, and support all depend on this record. Location pings are not the trip. If the app dies, the store still knows who was assigned. Every transition should be recorded with who caused it so a dispute can be reconstructed.

Core concepts in this module

  • State machine
  • Durable source of truth
  • Compare-and-set
  • Audit trail

How the modules work together

Drivers stream location points into ingest, which updates cells in the geo index. A rider request creates a trip in a requested state. Dispatch queries nearby cells, filters busy drivers, asks routing for ETAs, and attempts to lock one driver. The trip store is the authority: a compare-and-set changes the trip to assigned. Both apps subscribe to trip status. If the driver never accepts, the lease expires and dispatch tries again with a wider radius.

sections.label: WhatsApp
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Chat feels instantaneous, but the network is not. People switch from wifi to mobile, lose signal in elevators, and expect a message that left their phone to arrive later. A WhatsApp-style system is a connection fabric plus durable per-device queues. Presence and typing are hints; message history is truth.

System blueprint

Erlang-style designs shine here because each connection can be a lightweight process. The architectural lesson is more general: isolate connections from durable delivery.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Connection gateway

This module holds millions of sockets. It authenticates a device, keeps a session, and forwards bytes to the router. It should store as little durable state as possible so you can add or restart gateways. When a phone reconnects, the gateway helps the client resume from a cursor rather than replaying the entire history. Health checks must distinguish 'process up' from 'can still push messages'.

Core concepts in this module

  • Long-lived connections
  • Session resume
  • Horizontal gateways
  • Backpressure

2. Message router

The router is the delivery brain. It looks up devices for a user, writes the message once, and places work on each device queue. It does not need the plaintext if end-to-end encryption is in use; it routes envelopes. Ordering is per conversation, not global. Fan-out to a large group should be asynchronous so the sender is not blocked on the slowest member.

Core concepts in this module

  • Per-device queues
  • Envelope routing
  • Conversation ordering
  • Group fan-out

3. Receipt and presence services

Delivery and read receipts are themselves messages with a small payload. They must be idempotent because acks are retried. Presence is a TTL map: last seen, or a short 'online' flag. Mixing presence into the durable message table wastes writes and creates false precision. Users understand 'last seen recently' better than a blinking lie.

Core concepts in this module

  • Idempotent acks
  • Read receipts
  • TTL presence
  • Eventual status

4. Message store and offline queues

The store keeps conversation history and media pointers. Offline queues keep what has not been acknowledged by a device. Those are different retention rules. A queue can drop a payload after the device acknowledges; the store may keep it for new-device linking depending on the product. Encryption and multi-device pairing constrain what the server is allowed to read or re-encrypt.

Core concepts in this module

  • Durable history
  • Ack-based deletion
  • Multi-device
  • Media pointers

How the modules work together

A sender uploads an encrypted payload to its gateway. The router persists the message and enqueues it for each recipient device. If the device is connected, the gateway pushes it immediately and waits for a delivery ack. If not, the offline queue holds it. Read receipts are separate events so a lost ack does not resend forever. Presence updates expire quickly and are not written as permanent rows for every blink of connectivity.

sections.label: LinkedIn
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A professional feed is an event-driven ranking system on top of a connection graph. The write is 'someone posted or interacted.' The read is 'show me a small set of items I am likely to care about, without violating privacy.' Kafka-style logs let many consumers reuse the same activity: feed, notifications, search, and analytics.

System blueprint

The graph tells you who could see an item. Ranking tells you who should see it now. Those jobs should not share one synchronous service call.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Activity publisher

This module records the user action and appends an event with a stable ID. The event is the contract. If it is incomplete, every downstream job is wrong. Use an outbox so the database write and the log write do not diverge. The publisher should not rank the feed. Its success metric is durable, ordered, replayable activity.

Core concepts in this module

  • Event outbox
  • Stable event IDs
  • Replay
  • Contract versioning

2. Connection graph service

The graph stores who is connected, who follows whom, and which organizations a person belongs to. Feed and notifications query it, but they should not run unbounded traversals on the request path. Common questions become explicit APIs: first-degree connections, followers of this actor, members of this page. Privacy edges change, so consumers must be able to drop candidates that are no longer allowed.

Core concepts in this module

  • Graph APIs
  • Bounded traversal
  • Privacy edges
  • Membership

3. Candidate generation and ranker

Candidate generation is recall: gather more items than you will show. Ranking is precision: order them. Features include author affinity, recency, and inferred topics. Because models change, store the model version with the score. Ranking is expensive, so do it asynchronously for the next session when you can, and keep a cache of the last good list.

Core concepts in this module

  • Recall vs precision
  • Feature store
  • Model versioning
  • Feed cache

4. Kafka log

The log decouples producers from consumers. Feed builders, notification workers, and metrics can move at different speeds. Offsets make replay possible when a ranker is rewritten. Partition by actor or event type so related activity stays ordered. A log is not a database; consumers still need their own derived stores.

Core concepts in this module

  • Pub/sub log
  • Consumer offsets
  • Partition keys
  • Derived read models

How the modules work together

A post or comment is written and emitted to the log. Candidate generation walks or samples the graph and writes possible feed entries. The ranker scores those entries with features from the feature store. A feed request reads a ranked slice, applies privacy again, and caches it briefly. Notifications and search consume the same log with their own offsets. If ranking is slow, the feed can show a simpler recency list rather than fail.

sections.label: Instagram
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Photo sharing combines a social graph, a media pipeline, and a feed. The image bytes are large and cacheable. The metadata is small and frequently queried. IDs must be unique across shards and roughly sortable by time so feeds can page without asking every shard for 'latest.'

System blueprint

Sharding is usually by user. That makes 'posts by this author' easy and 'global latest' hard, which is the right trade if the product is a personal feed.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Media pipeline

This worker turns an original into thumbnails and display sizes. It should be asynchronous so the upload API returns quickly. Variants use new keys so a retry cannot serve a half-resized image. Strip GPS and other sensitive metadata unless the product explicitly keeps it. Failures retry from the original object.

Core concepts in this module

  • Async derivatives
  • Immutable variants
  • EXIF hygiene
  • Retry from original

2. Feed service

The feed is a list of post IDs plus enough author data to render a cell. It can be precomputed for active users or merged at read time for sparse graphs. Celebrity fan-out has the same push/pull tension as Twitter. Authorization is rechecked on read because a switched account from public to private should not keep appearing in caches.

Core concepts in this module

  • Inbox vs fan-in
  • Post pointers
  • Rechecked privacy
  • Active-user materialization

3. ID generator

A good photo ID is unique, compact, and roughly increasing with time. Snowflake-style IDs encode a timestamp and a machine identity so shards can generate IDs without a central lock. Random UUIDs work for uniqueness but make 'give me newer than X' clumsy and fragment indexes. The generator must survive clock skew and process restarts without collisions.

Core concepts in this module

  • Snowflake IDs
  • Time-sortable keys
  • Allocation ranges
  • Clock safety

4. Metadata shards and object storage

User-sharded metadata keeps an author's posts together. Object storage and the CDN carry the bytes. The follow graph decides feed membership. Cross-shard operations, such as a global report or a celebrity lookup, need their own access path. Plan how you will move a user when a shard overheats; that is harder than picking the first hash function.

Core concepts in this module

  • User sharding
  • Object + CDN
  • Hot users
  • Resharding

How the modules work together

The client uploads bytes to object storage, then calls the API with the object key. The ID generator issues a time-sortable ID. Metadata is written to the author's shard. The media pipeline creates thumbnails and a CDN-friendly variant. Feed delivery either pushes the post ID to follower inboxes or pulls recent posts from followed authors at read time. Deleted or hidden media must invalidate CDN paths, not only the metadata row.

sections.label: Facebook social graph
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A social network is a graph of objects and associations: people, pages, posts, likes, memberships. Most product screens are a few named traversals, not arbitrary graph queries. TAO-style systems put a cache-aware graph layer in front of storage so 'friends of this user' stays fast while still having a durable backend.

System blueprint

Design the API around associations you will actually query. A general graph database query language on the request path is usually the wrong starting point for this product.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Graph API

This is the product contract: get object, get associations, create edge, delete edge. It enforces authentication and privacy, paginates large edge lists, and hides storage layout. If every app writes SQL against the edge table, you will never change sharding. Keep result sizes bounded; 'all friends of friends' is a request you should refuse or precompute.

Core concepts in this module

  • Named traversals
  • Privacy checks
  • Bounded pagination
  • API as facade

2. TAO-style cache layer

TAO popularized a two-level approach: a cache that understands objects and associations, backed by a sharded store. Reads go to the cache; writes go to storage and then invalidate. The cache is not just Redis-as-blob. It knows the graph operations, so it can serve 'assoc get' without assembling a response from many keys in the client.

Core concepts in this module

  • Association cache
  • Read-heavy graph
  • Write-through / invalidate
  • Hot objects

3. Association service and stores

Objects have a type and payload. Edges have a type, from-id, to-id, and time. Storage is sharded so a popular object's edges can be split. Secondary indexes support lookups in the reverse direction, such as 'pages this user likes.' Consistency matters most for privacy edges: a removed friend should not keep seeing cached content.

Core concepts in this module

  • Object/edge model
  • Reverse indexes
  • Sharded edge lists
  • Privacy consistency

4. Invalidation bus

After a write, caches must learn that an edge changed. A lightweight invalidation message is usually better than pushing full objects everywhere. Consumers drop or reload one association list. If invalidations are lost, a TTL remains as a safety net. Version numbers help a reader detect that a cached edge list is older than a write it just performed.

Core concepts in this module

  • Cache invalidation
  • Version tokens
  • TTL safety net
  • Lost-update protection

How the modules work together

A product request asks for an object and a typed edge list, such as members or reactions. The cache layer returns hot data and fills from storage on miss. Writes update storage, then publish invalidations so caches drop or version the changed edges. Privacy is applied at the graph API, not only in the client. Popular objects, such as a major page, need extra caching and careful write batching to avoid a hot partition.

sections.label: Dropbox / Google Drive
sections.html:
What this system is solving

File sync is a metadata problem dressed as a storage problem. The bytes can be split, hashed, and stored once. The hard work is reconciling trees across devices: renames, offline edits, deletes, and two people changing the same file. The blueprint stores chunks immutably and lets a metadata service decide what the current tree is.

System blueprint

Dedup is a storage optimization. Sync correctness comes from manifests, versions, and conflict rules, not from hashing alone.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Chunker and dedup

Files are split into chunks so a small edit does not re-upload a 2 GB video. Content hashes let the server skip bytes it already stores. Chunk size is a trade: tiny chunks increase metadata, huge chunks waste upload. Clients should encrypt or hash in a way that still allows the server to address chunks. This module must treat two identical PDFs from different users carefully if privacy requires per-namespace encryption.

Core concepts in this module

  • Content-defined chunking
  • Hash addressing
  • Upload resume
  • Namespace privacy

2. Sync engine and metadata

Metadata holds paths, permissions, versions, and the list of chunk hashes that make a file. Commits are transactional: a new tree either replaces the old one or is rejected as stale. Renames are metadata operations, not byte copies. Sharing a folder is an ACL change on a subtree, which is why metadata, not object storage, is the product database.

Core concepts in this module

  • Manifest commit
  • Optimistic versions
  • Rename as metadata
  • ACLs on trees

3. Notification service

Devices should not poll every few seconds. After a commit, this module wakes subscribed clients with a cursor. The client then fetches the delta. Notifications can be lossy if the cursor protocol is correct: a missed ping just means a later catch-up. This is cheaper and kinder to batteries than tight polling.

Core concepts in this module

  • Change notifications
  • Device cursors
  • Lossy ping, reliable delta
  • Wake vs poll

4. Chunk store and device cursors

The chunk store is append-only object storage. Device cursors remember how far each client has applied the tree. Tombstones record deletes so a device that was offline does not resurrect a file. Garbage collection is delayed and reference-counted. If you delete bytes when the first user removes a file, you may destroy a chunk another namespace still needs.

Core concepts in this module

  • Immutable chunks
  • Tombstones
  • Reference counting
  • Delayed GC

How the modules work together

A client hashes local chunks, asks which hashes the server already has, uploads the missing ones, and commits a new manifest for the file path. The metadata service assigns a version and notifies other devices. Those devices download missing chunks and apply the tree change. If two commits descend from the same parent, the service keeps a conflict copy instead of silently choosing. Garbage collection waits until no manifest references a chunk.

sections.label: URL shortener
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A shortener has two calls with opposite needs. Creating a link is a write with uniqueness and abuse checks. Opening a link is an extremely hot read that should be a single key lookup and a redirect. Analytics, preview pages, and custom aliases must stay off that redirect path unless you accept losing the performance that made the product useful.

System blueprint

The short key is the entire API. Generate it carefully, store it simply, and cache the hottest keys.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Key allocator

Keys can be random, hash-based, or issued from a counter encoded in base62. Random keys need enough bits to make collisions rare and a uniqueness check anyway. Hashing the destination makes the same URL collapse to one key, which may or may not be desired. Counters are simple but leak creation volume. Reserve custom aliases in the same transaction that writes the record.

Core concepts in this module

  • Key generation
  • Collision handling
  • Base62 encoding
  • Alias reservation

2. Redirect service and cache

This path should avoid joins, user profiles, and synchronous analytics. Read key, write a cache entry, return Location. Choose 301 if the mapping never changes, 302 if you need to keep seeing clicks at your edge. Signed or allow-listed destinations reduce phishing. A single viral key becomes a hot partition; replicate that entry widely instead of scaling the whole table.

Core concepts in this module

  • KV lookup
  • HTTP redirect semantics
  • Hot-key replication
  • Safety checks

3. Analytics

Clicks are a firehose. Drop them on a queue with the key, time, and coarse geography. Aggregate offline. If analytics is down, redirects should still work. Unique-click counts need a privacy-aware approximation, not a full replay of IP addresses in the request path.

Core concepts in this module

  • Async click events
  • Approximate counts
  • Privacy
  • Decoupled metrics

How the modules work together

A create request validates the destination, asks the allocator for a unique key, and writes the mapping. A redirect request hits the edge cache or the key-value store and returns 301 or 302. The click is appended to a queue for later counts. Custom aliases take a transactional reservation so two teams cannot claim the same word. If the cache is wrong, the store wins; if the store is down, fail the create, and decide explicitly whether redirects fail open from cache.

sections.label: Pastebin
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Pastebin is a small object store with public links, expiry, and a read-heavy traffic shape. Anyone can upload text; anyone with the link may read it. That combination makes abuse, accidental secrets, and sudden popularity the real design constraints. The body lives in object storage. Metadata answers whether the paste still exists and who may see it.

System blueprint

Expiry is both cleanup and authorization. A paste past its deadline must not be readable even if the blob is still on disk for a few minutes.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Paste service

This module issues IDs, enforces size limits, and stores metadata. Unlisted pastes rely on unguessable IDs; private pastes need a real owner check. Rendering must escape HTML so a paste cannot become a script on your domain. The service should not scan the entire object store to list a user's pastes; that is why metadata exists.

Core concepts in this module

  • Unguessable IDs
  • Size limits
  • Safe rendering
  • Visibility modes

2. Abuse filter

Open upload is a spam magnet. Rate-limit by IP and account, detect malware or banned patterns, and require a challenge when volume spikes. Filters will be wrong sometimes, so keep an appeal or override path for trusted users. Do not wait for a human to review every paste before it is reachable if the product is 'instant share,' but do keep takedown fast.

Core concepts in this module

  • Rate limits
  • Content scanning
  • Takedown path
  • Challenge / CAPTCHA

3. Expiry sweeper

A background job lists pastes whose deadline has passed, removes metadata, and deletes objects. Because jobs lag, the read path must also compare now to expiry. Storage lifecycle policies catch blobs the sweeper missed. Log deletions so you can explain why a link died.

Core concepts in this module

  • TTL as policy
  • Read-time expiry
  • Lifecycle rules
  • Idempotent delete

4. Read cache and object storage

Popular pastes become hot keys. Cache the body and the metadata together so you do not serve a cached body after metadata says expired. Object storage holds the canonical bytes. Short pastes may live only in the database, but a single rule—'bodies in object storage'—is easier to operate once size grows.

Core concepts in this module

  • Read-heavy caching
  • Coupled cache keys
  • Object durability
  • Hot pastes

How the modules work together

A create call runs through abuse checks, stores the body under a random ID, and writes metadata with size, visibility, and expiry. A read loads metadata first. If the paste is expired or private, the service returns not found. Otherwise it serves from cache or storage and never executes the paste as HTML. A sweeper later deletes metadata and then the blob. Lifecycle rules on the bucket are a backup, not the only control.

sections.label: Rate limiter
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A rate limiter is a policy engine in front of expensive work. It answers whether this caller may proceed now. The algorithm you pick encodes the product rule: token bucket allows bursts, sliding window smooths traffic, fixed window is simple and slightly unfair at boundaries. In a fleet of gateways the hard part is shared state and failure policy.

System blueprint

If the limiter store is down you must choose fail-open or fail-closed. That choice is part of the design, not an afterthought.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Identity

Limits are meaningless if the key is wrong. Anonymous traffic uses IP and TLS fingerprints with care; authenticated traffic uses the user or API key. Expensive routes get their own key suffix so a cheap health check does not share budget with an export job. Identity must be cheap; a limiter that calls a remote user service on every request becomes the outage.

Core concepts in this module

  • Caller keys
  • Route-specific budgets
  • Cheap identification
  • Multi-tenant fairness

2. Limiter decision

This module implements the algorithm. Token bucket stores a balance and a last refill time. Sliding window stores counts in time slots. The update must be atomic across gateways, usually with Redis-style scripts or compare-and-set. Return a retry-after with jitter so rejected clients do not retry in lockstep. Document what happens when this module cannot reach the store.

Core concepts in this module

  • Token bucket
  • Sliding window
  • Atomic counters
  • Jittered retry-after

3. Policy config

Policies change without a redeploy: 100 requests per minute for free users, 10 per second for search, a temporary ban. Store them in a small config with versions. Operators need an emergency switch. Keep the number of policies small enough that every request does not evaluate a novel.

Core concepts in this module

  • Versioned policies
  • Emergency kill switch
  • Per-tier limits
  • Composable rules

4. Counter store and metrics

State is tiny and extremely hot. Use memory-speed storage with replication and short TTLs so dead keys vanish. Metrics should show reject rate by key class, not only totals, or you will miss a single abusive tenant. Do not log every decision at full cardinality; sample.

Core concepts in this module

  • Distributed counters
  • Hot-key storage
  • TTL hygiene
  • Reject metrics

How the modules work together

The gateway extracts a key such as user, API token, or IP. The decision module reads policy, performs an atomic increment or token consume, and returns allow or retry-after. Metrics record both results. The application runs only on allow. Policies can stack: a global IP limit and a tighter limit on the search endpoint. Clock sources must be server-side so clients cannot reset their budget.

sections.label: Ticketmaster / BookMyShow
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Ticketing is inventory under a flash sale. Many people want the same seats at the same instant. The browser cannot own a seat. A hold is a short lease in a transactional inventory service, and payment is a later step that must not create a second sale if the client retries. An admission queue protects the database from becoming the waiting room.

System blueprint

If two checkouts can both mark seat A12 sold, the rest of the architecture does not matter. Start from a unique constraint or conditional update on the seat.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Waiting room

This is load management, not shopping. It issues a signed token when a browser may enter checkout. The release rate matches inventory and payment capacity. Without it, you scale the storefront into a self-inflicted outage. The waiting room should be simple and separately scalable: it does not browse every seat map.

Core concepts in this module

  • Admission control
  • Signed entry tokens
  • Release rate
  • Flash-sale shedding

2. Inventory and seat lock

Each seat has a state: available, held, sold. A hold writes who owns it and when it expires. The write uses a condition so only one holder wins. Holds are short because abandoned browsers are common. Extending a hold is an explicit call, not an infinite reservation. Seat maps can be cached for display, but the lock always goes to the authority.

Core concepts in this module

  • Conditional updates
  • Short leases
  • Cached map, authoritative lock
  • Expiry workers

3. Payment and order service

Payment is slow and retries. The order record must survive a double callback. Convert hold to sold only after the processor confirms, and store the processor reference. The user-visible confirmation is derived from order state, not from the last browser response. This is a small saga: hold, charge, sell, or compensate.

Core concepts in this module

  • Idempotent payment
  • Order state machine
  • Compensation
  • Webhook races

How the modules work together

Users receive a place in the waiting room and are admitted at a rate the core can handle. Selecting seats creates a hold with an expiry. Payment uses an idempotency key. On success the order service converts the hold to sold. A sweeper releases expired holds. If payment succeeds after the hold expired, reconciliation must either restore the seat sale or refund; it must not silently drop the money.

sections.label: Airbnb
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Marketplace lodging has a soft search problem and a hard booking problem. Search can be a little stale. A double-booked apartment cannot. Availability calendars, ranking, and payments therefore live in different modules, and the booking path re-validates dates against a transactional store even if search showed the listing as open.

System blueprint

Think of search as advertising and booking as inventory. The advertisement can lag; the inventory cannot.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Search ranking

Ranking mixes quality, price, location, and business goals. It reads a denormalized listing index, not the reservation table. That keeps search fast and independently scalable. Because the index lags, the UI should treat results as candidates. Filters such as 'entire home' belong in the index; 'available these exact dates' should be rechecked at booking even if also used as a search filter.

Core concepts in this module

  • Denormalized index
  • Multi-signal ranking
  • Stale availability
  • Candidate vs commit

2. Calendar

The calendar captures host rules: min stay, blocked dates, preparation time. It is the input to availability, not the reservation itself. Modeling this as per-listing date rows or ranges is a product choice with different update costs. Calendar edits must not silently erase existing reservations; they only change what new guests can book.

Core concepts in this module

  • Availability rules
  • Range vs per-day rows
  • Host constraints
  • Non-destructive edits

3. Booking service

Booking inserts a reservation with a constraint that prevents overlapping stays, or it locks the listing dates in a transaction. It then starts payment as a saga. The guest receives a reservation ID immediately. Everything else—emails, search updates, host payouts—follows from events. Two guests clicking the same weekend is the race this module exists to win exactly once.

Core concepts in this module

  • Exclusion constraints
  • Booking saga
  • Reservation ID
  • Race to lock

4. Payments

Money may be authorized at request and captured after host acceptance, depending on the product. Payouts to hosts are delayed on purpose. Each movement needs a ledger entry and an idempotency key. Booking state and payment state can disagree briefly; a reconciler, not the guest refresh button, fixes that.

Core concepts in this module

  • Auth vs capture
  • Idempotency
  • Delayed payouts
  • Reconciliation

How the modules work together

Hosts publish listings and calendar rules. An indexer builds documents for search. Guests query ranking, then start a booking. Booking locks the date range, starts payment, and commits a reservation. Events update the search document so the listing disappears for those nights. If payment fails, the lock expires. Host cancellations and guest cancellations are explicit transitions with refund rules, not deletes of history.
