sections.label: Amazon e-commerce
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Retail checkout is a long-running workflow across catalog, cart, inventory, payment, and fulfillment. No single database transaction spans the warehouse and the card network. The order becomes a saga: a durable state machine with steps and compensations. Inventory is reserved, not guessed from a cached count on the product page.

System blueprint

A sold-out badge on the storefront is a hint. The reservation at checkout is the decision.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Cart

The cart is a working document. It survives devices through an account ID or a signed cookie. It can hold items that later go out of stock. Do not put payment authorization in the cart. Price the cart at checkout time because promotions change. Merge guest and user carts carefully to avoid losing items or leaking another person's basket.

Core concepts in this module

  • Durable intent
  • Price at checkout
  • Cart merge
  • No hard reservation

2. Inventory

Inventory is a ledger of on-hand, reserved, and shipped units per SKU and location. Reservations use conditional decrements. Oversell happens when you decrement a cache. Multi-warehouse routing is a later choice; correctness starts with one atomic reservation record. Expired reservations return stock to the pool.

Core concepts in this module

  • Reservation ledger
  • Conditional decrement
  • Reservation TTL
  • Location-level stock

3. Order workflow

The order ID is the customer's handle on the saga. States include created, paid, allocated, shipped, and canceled. Each step records a command result so retries do not charge twice or ship twice. An outbox publishes events for email, fraud, and warehouse systems. Humans in support need the same state machine; they should not edit stock by folklore.

Core concepts in this module

  • Sagas
  • Order state machine
  • Outbox events
  • Compensation

4. Payment and fulfillment

Payment talks to a processor with idempotency keys. Fulfillment assigns warehouses, packing, and carriers. These modules should accept commands from the order workflow, not invent their own order IDs. Tracking numbers flow back as events. Partial shipment is a first-class state, not an exception buried in notes.

Core concepts in this module

  • Idempotent capture
  • Warehouse allocation
  • Partial shipment
  • Event callbacks

How the modules work together

Browsing hits cached catalog. Adding to cart writes intent, often without a hard reservation. Checkout creates an order, reserves stock, authorizes payment, and emits events. Fulfillment allocates a warehouse and later ships. If payment fails, reservations release. If an item cannot ship, compensation refunds or splits the order. The customer sees order state derived from the log, not from whatever page they last posted.

sections.label: Web crawler
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A crawler is a distributed scheduler that downloads the web without becoming a denial-of-service tool. The frontier decides what to fetch next. Politeness limits how hard you hit one host. Dedup stops you from fetching the same page through a thousand URLs. Workers are replaceable; the frontier and seen-set are the system.

System blueprint

If you only remember one rule, remember per-host concurrency. Throughput without politeness is just abuse.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. URL frontier

The frontier is a prioritized, partitioned queue of work. Priority might be site importance, recency, or change rate. Partition by host so one site cannot occupy every worker. Leases prevent two fetchers from taking the same URL. When a worker dies, the lease expires and the URL returns. This is the difference between a queue and a lost-work pile.

Core concepts in this module

  • Prioritized queues
  • Host partitions
  • Work leases
  • Replay on timeout

2. Politeness

Politeness reads robots.txt, crawl-delay, and your own per-host QPS budget. It is a gate in front of the fetcher, not a comment in a design doc. Some hosts need even stricter limits after errors. Identify your crawler honestly. Ignore this module and you will be banned, sued, or both, and your data will be biased toward whoever failed to block you.

Core concepts in this module

  • robots.txt
  • Per-host QPS
  • Backoff on errors
  • Honest user-agent

3. Dedup and parser

Canonicalization strips tracking query params and session IDs before hashing. Dedup can use an exact store for recent URLs and a Bloom filter for the long tail. The parser extracts links and language, and it must bound HTML size so a huge page cannot explode memory. Content hashes detect that two URLs are the same document.

Core concepts in this module

  • URL canonicalization
  • Bloom filters
  • Content hashes
  • Bounded parse

4. Fetcher fleet and content store

Fetchers are stateless HTTP clients with timeouts, size limits, and sandboxing. They write raw content and fetch metadata: status, headers, time. The store is append-oriented so you can recrawl and keep history. Do not run JavaScript in the fetcher unless you have an isolated renderer farm; that is a different, more expensive module.

Core concepts in this module

  • Timeouts and size caps
  • Stateless workers
  • Fetch metadata
  • Optional render farm

How the modules work together

Operators load seeds. The frontier leases URLs to fetchers that respect robots rules and host budgets. Successful fetches go to content storage and to a parser. The parser extracts links, canonicalizes them, and asks dedup whether each URL is new. New URLs re-enter the frontier with a priority. Failures retry with backoff or go to a dead-letter queue. The seen index must be huge and approximate-tolerant; a rare re-fetch is better than unbounded growth.

sections.label: Search autocomplete
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Autocomplete must answer in a few tens of milliseconds as a person types. That rules out a general search of the catalog on every keystroke. The system keeps a compact prefix index in memory, a small top-K list per prefix, and a cache for the hottest prefixes. Freshness is handled by rebuilding versions offline.

System blueprint

The online path only reads. Writers publish a new immutable index and flip a pointer.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Suggest API and cache

This path is latency-critical. Cap prefix length, result count, and payload size. Cache full responses for popular prefixes such as 'a' or 'app' with a short TTL. The API should be read-only and cheap to clone in every region. Language and market belong in the cache key or you will suggest the wrong store.

Core concepts in this module

  • Tight SLIs
  • Prefix cache
  • Locale keys
  • Result caps

2. Trie / FST lookup

A trie or finite-state transducer maps a prefix to a small set of completions in memory. This is why autocomplete is fast. The structure is built offline because updating a huge trie in place on the request path is painful. Compact representations matter; the whole hot index should fit in RAM on each replica.

Core concepts in this module

  • Tries
  • Finite-state indexes
  • Memory residency
  • Immutable versions

3. Top-K ranker

Many words share a prefix. You return only a handful. Ranking uses frequency, click-through, recency, and business rules. Safety filters remove spam and offensive completions. Personalization, if any, must be a cheap re-rank of a tiny list, not a new index walk.

Core concepts in this module

  • Top-K
  • Frequency signals
  • Safety filters
  • Light personalization

4. Index builder

Batch jobs read query logs and catalog titles, clean them, and emit a new index artifact. Building is expensive and can fail; never mutate the live structure halfway. Atomic swap keeps the online path simple. Keep one previous version for rollback when a bad dictionary ships.

Core concepts in this module

  • Offline build
  • Atomic swap
  • Rollback version
  • Log-derived dictionaries

How the modules work together

The client debounces slightly and sends the current prefix. The API checks a tiny cache, then queries the in-memory index for completions. A ranker orders them by frequency, freshness, and safety. Offline, query logs and catalog changes build the next index version. A process loads the new version and then serves it. Bad terms are filtered before they ever reach the client.

sections.label: Spotify
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Music streaming looks like video streaming with smaller files and a stronger catalog of user-made playlists. Playback should work even if the recommendation model is unhappy. Audio segments are cacheable. Playlist edits are metadata. Listening history is an event stream that later trains recommendations.

System blueprint

A skipped song is an event, not a reason to stall the next segment.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. License token and playback API

Rights differ by country, device, and subscription. This module issues a short-lived token that the CDN or player can verify. It is also where offline download grants are recorded. Keep it independent from recommendation so billing and licensing outages are visible and rare, not tangled with a model release.

Core concepts in this module

  • Entitlement
  • Short-lived tokens
  • Territory rules
  • Offline grants

2. Audio CDN

Tracks are encoded at a few bitrates and stored as objects. Popular tracks should already be at the edge. The player can switch bitrate between segments. Because tracks are smaller than movies, caching is easier, but catalog size is huge; not everything can be hot. Origin fill and popularity-based prewarm still matter.

Core concepts in this module

  • Multi-bitrate audio
  • Edge cache
  • Popularity prewarm
  • Segment fetch

3. Playlists

A playlist is an ordered list of track IDs with collaborators and a version. Concurrent edits need a version check or CRDT-like list if many people edit at once. The playlist is not the audio. Sharing a playlist shares metadata and entitlements, not a zip of files.

Core concepts in this module

  • Ordered lists
  • Collaborative versions
  • Track pointers
  • Cache of playlist JSON

4. Recommendations and listen stream

Every play, skip, and completion is an event. Pipelines build features and candidate lists. The online service should read prepared rankings and apply a few rules, not train a model on the request. Deduplicate events so a retried client does not convince you someone looped a track 400 times.

Core concepts in this module

  • Listen events
  • Nearline features
  • Prepared rankings
  • Event dedup

How the modules work together

The player asks for a license and a list of CDN hosts, then fetches encrypted segments. Playlist changes update the playlist database and invalidate a small cache. Listens go to a stream used for history and models. Recommendations compute offline and nearline; the home screen reads a prepared list. If recommendations fail, recently played and downloaded titles still work.

sections.label: Slack / Discord
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Team chat is real-time fan-out plus durable history. People expect a message to appear in every open client and to still be there tomorrow after a laptop sleeps. Gateways hold WebSockets. A message service persists first, then publishes. Presence and typing are ephemeral so they do not drown the database.

System blueprint

If a client can reconnect and catch up from a sequence number, you can lose a gateway without losing the conversation.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. WebSocket gateway

Gateways terminate sockets, authenticate, and subscribe the connection to a set of channels. They should be stateless relative to message history. Shard connections by user so a person does not split events across machines without a plan. Heartbeats detect dead phones. This layer is where you apply per-connection backpressure.

Core concepts in this module

  • WebSockets
  • Connection sharding
  • Heartbeats
  • Slow-consumer handling

2. Message API and store

The API is the write authority: permissions, attachments, edits, deletes. Messages get a monotonic sequence per channel. Edits and deletes are new events against that ID so late subscribers converge. Search is a derived index, not the store itself. Large channels need pagination that is stable as new messages arrive.

Core concepts in this module

  • Per-channel sequence
  • Edit/delete events
  • Permissioned writes
  • Stable history pages

3. Channel router and pub/sub

Pub/sub carries live events to gateways. A channel with hundreds of thousands of members cannot be a single process doing a for-loop. Fan-out trees, partition the channel, or push to online members only and let others catch up. Membership changes must subscribe and unsubscribe gateways without dropping the persist step.

Core concepts in this module

  • Pub/sub fan-out
  • Online vs history
  • Membership updates
  • Partitioned channels

4. Presence and notifications

Typing indicators and online flags expire in seconds and should live in memory. Notifications go to devices that have no socket: push, email, or desktop. They must respect mute and mention rules. A notification is a derived event from a persisted message, so retries use the message ID.

Core concepts in this module

  • Ephemeral presence
  • Mute rules
  • Push fan-out
  • Derived notifications

How the modules work together

A send call persists a message with a channel sequence, then publishes to the bus. Gateways subscribed to that channel push to connected clients. Offline users get a notification. On reconnect, the client asks for messages after its last sequence. Slow clients are disconnected from live push and told to catch up in batch so one bad laptop does not stall the channel.

sections.label: Zoom / Google Meet
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A meeting is a latency-sensitive media graph. Signaling sets up the room. WebRTC moves audio and video. An SFU forwards streams without mixing every tile into one video, which scales better than an MCU that composites a single layout on the server. Quality is managed continuously through estimates of loss and bandwidth.

System blueprint

If you mix every participant into one server-side video, you pay encode cost on the server for every layout. An SFU forwards selected streams and lets the client decide what to decode.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Signaling and meeting control

Signaling exchanges join, leave, SDP offers, and ice candidates. Meeting control applies host policies: mute all, lock the room, admit from lobby. This path is not the video. It must be highly available, but its bandwidth is small. Store just enough session state to reconnect a client that refreshed the tab without creating a second ghost participant.

Core concepts in this module

  • WebRTC signaling
  • SDP / ICE
  • Room policy
  • Rejoin state

2. SFU media servers

A Selective Forwarding Unit receives each sender's stream and forwards it to subscribers. It can drop a video layer when a viewer has little bandwidth instead of transcoding a full MCU layout. Place SFUs regionally. Admission control matters: a 500-person webinar is a different topology from a 3-person standup. Monitor packet loss, jitter, and RTT per stream.

Core concepts in this module

  • SFU vs MCU
  • Simulcast / layers
  • Regional placement
  • Admission limits

3. TURN fallback

Some corporate networks block peer-to-peer. TURN relays media through a server you control. It is expensive, so it is a fallback, not the default. Health checks should prove that a client can reach at least one relay before you promise a meeting. Capacity here is a classic overflow pool.

Core concepts in this module

  • NAT traversal
  • Relay cost
  • Fallback only
  • Reachability checks

4. Recording and quality logs

Recording subscribes like a hidden participant or taps the SFU. Write media to object storage in chunks so a crash loses seconds, not the hour. Quality logs (loss, bitrate, device) are analytics and should never block sending the next packet. Compliance may require consent flags before this module is allowed to start.

Core concepts in this module

  • Recording as subscriber
  • Chunked storage
  • QoS telemetry
  • Consent

How the modules work together

A client joins through signaling, receives meeting credentials, and negotiates WebRTC with an SFU in a nearby region. Media packets flow to the SFU, which forwards them to other participants. TURN is used only when direct or peer-reflexive paths fail. Meeting control handles mute, lobby, and host actions as small messages. Recording is a separate subscriber so a recorder crash does not end the live call.

sections.label: Google Maps
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Maps combine a static, cacheable picture of the world with a dynamic routing problem. Tiles are versioned images or vectors for each zoom and coordinate. Routing searches a road graph. Traffic updates the weights on that graph without forcing every phone to download a new planet.

System blueprint

Do not rebuild tiles because a highway slowed down. Tiles are geography; traffic is a stream of weights.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Tile service and CDN

The world is cut into tiles at many zoom levels. Each tile is immutable for a map version, which makes CDNs happy. Clients request only what is on screen plus a small prefetch. A new map release is a new version prefix, not an edit in place. Vector tiles move styling to the client; raster tiles are simpler images. Either way, the key is z/x/y plus version.

Core concepts in this module

  • Tile pyramids
  • Immutable versions
  • Viewport fetch
  • CDN cache keys

2. Routing

Routing is a shortest-path search on a graph of road segments. Hierarchical techniques and contraction hierarchies keep city-scale queries fast. Alternate routes are bounded; you do not enumerate every path. Partition graphs so a regional replica can answer without loading the planet into one process. When traffic data is missing, fall back to free-flow speeds.

Core concepts in this module

  • Road graphs
  • Shortest path
  • Graph partitions
  • Bounded alternatives

3. Traffic

Probes from phones and historical averages update edge weights. This is a stream. Publish snapshots or deltas to routing replicas. Do not wait for a perfect global picture; a slightly stale weight is better than no route. Extreme incidents can also trigger reroute pushes to active navigations.

Core concepts in this module

  • Probe streams
  • Weight updates
  • Historical priors
  • Reroute signals

4. Places

Businesses and landmarks live in a geo index with attributes such as hours and category. This is closer to nearby search than to tile rendering. Ranking mixes distance and relevance. Hours can be stale, so show freshness and let the details page re-fetch. Places writes should not block tile reads.

Core concepts in this module

  • Geo documents
  • Distance + relevance
  • Freshness labels
  • Decoupled writes

How the modules work together

The client asks for tiles covering the viewport and, separately, for a route. Tiles come from a versioned pyramid at the edge. Routing loads a graph partition, applies traffic weights, and returns a polyline plus ETA. Places search uses a geo index for businesses. Navigation keeps requesting traffic deltas, not a new set of basemap tiles, as the car moves.

sections.label: Food delivery (Swiggy)
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Food delivery coordinates three parties who do not share a process: customer, restaurant, and rider. The order is a state machine. Kitchen time and travel time are estimates that change. Assignment is a smaller version of ride dispatch, with the extra constraint that food is cooling on a counter.

System blueprint

The customer app should read order state, not compute it from independent restaurant and rider APIs.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Order lifecycle

This is the product database: placed, accepted, preparing, assigned, picked up, delivered, canceled. Every other module emits events; this module decides whether the transition is legal. Support tools should replay this log. Do not delete a canceled order; you need it for refunds and disputes. Timeouts matter: an unaccepted order cannot sit forever.

Core concepts in this module

  • Shared state machine
  • Legal transitions
  • Timeouts
  • Support replay

2. Kitchen / restaurant

Restaurants accept, reject, and update prep time. Their systems are unreliable, so the app or a tablet POS should use idempotent commands. Menu and item availability belong here and should flow to the customer catalog asynchronously. A restaurant going offline mid-order is a first-class event, not an error string.

Core concepts in this module

  • Accept / reject
  • Prep-time signals
  • Menu availability
  • Partner unreliability

3. Dispatch and rider geo

Assignment looks like Uber: geo cells, short leases, one rider one order (or a planned batch). Food adds stacking rules and pickup windows. A rider who accepts but never moves must be reassigned. Keep location data hot and the assignment durable on the order.

Core concepts in this module

  • Geo matching
  • Assignment leases
  • Batching rules
  • Reassignment timers

4. ETA and payments

ETA is kitchen remaining plus travel, with uncertainty. Show a range when inputs are poor. Payments usually authorize up front and capture on success, with refunds on cancel. Promos and delivery fees belong on the order, not only on a receipt PDF. Do not let the rider app invent prices.

Core concepts in this module

  • Composite ETA
  • Uncertainty ranges
  • Auth / capture / refund
  • Priced on the order

How the modules work together

A customer places an order and pays. The restaurant accepts and later marks food ready. Dispatch searches nearby riders and leases one. Rider location updates refresh ETA. If the restaurant rejects or the rider vanishes, the order service transitions and may reassign or cancel with a refund. Notifications are derived from those transitions so the three apps do not invent conflicting stories.

sections.label: Payment system (Stripe)
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A payment API must survive retries, ambiguous processor answers, and months of disputes. The user-facing charge is a state machine. The money movement is an append-only ledger. Idempotency keys make 'click twice' safe. Reconciliation assumes that your records and the card network will disagree and provides a job to explain the difference.

System blueprint

If you only store a mutable 'balance' column, you cannot audit a charge. Always keep the journal.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Payments API and idempotency

The public contract is a payment object and a key the merchant repeats on retry. The first request stores the key and the eventual response. A second request with the same key returns the same object even if the first call timed out after the processor accepted the charge. Without this, you double-bill. Keys need a retention window and a hash of the request so a reused key with different amounts is rejected.

Core concepts in this module

  • Idempotency keys
  • Stable payment objects
  • Timeout races
  • Request hashing

2. Authorization

This module talks to card networks or banks. It models auth, capture, void, refund, and dispute as separate states. Network errors are not failures you can guess; you may need to query the processor or wait for a callback. Never invent a success because a library threw a timeout. Map processor codes into your own state so merchants do not learn every bank's dialect.

Core concepts in this module

  • Auth vs capture
  • Processor ambiguity
  • State mapping
  • Query-on-timeout

3. Ledger

A ledger is append-only entries that must balance. Available and pending balances are views over those entries. Fees, refunds, and chargebacks are new entries, not edits. This is how you answer 'why did this payout change' six months later. Double-entry is not ceremony; it is how money systems stay explainable.

Core concepts in this module

  • Append-only journal
  • Double-entry
  • Derived balances
  • Immutable corrections

4. Webhooks and reconciliation

Webhooks are at-least-once and can arrive out of order. Sign them, include an event ID, and tell merchants to be idempotent. Reconciliation compares processor settlement files to ledger totals. Differences are normal: timing, fees, partial refunds. A human-readable exception queue is part of the design. Do not 'fix' a mismatch by secretly editing yesterday's entry.

Core concepts in this module

  • Signed webhooks
  • At-least-once events
  • Settlement files
  • Exception queues

How the modules work together

Checkout sends a charge with an idempotency key. Authorization talks to the processor and records an attempt. Ledger entries capture the merchant, customer, fees, and pending vs captured amounts. The API returns a stable payment object. Webhooks notify the merchant of the same state. Nightly files from the processor are compared to the ledger; mismatches become tickets, not silent balance edits.

sections.label: Notification service
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Notifications look like 'send a message,' but the system is a router across push, email, and SMS with preferences, priority, and limited retries. The product emits an intent. Channel workers talk to vendors. A user who opted out of marketing must still receive a security code. Those are different pipelines, not a boolean.

System blueprint

A notification is not sent until preferences, templates, and idempotency keys say it should be. Vendors fail; your attempt log is the memory.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Notify API and router

The API accepts an intent, not a raw vendor payload. The router chooses channels, drops opted-out marketing, and enforces a dedup key so a retried order event does not SMS twice. Priority selects a queue. This is also where you reject unknown templates before they become poison pills in workers.

Core concepts in this module

  • Intent vs send
  • Dedup keys
  • Preference checks
  • Priority queues

2. Templates

Templates keep copy and layout out of every microservice. They need versioning, locale, and a strict variable schema so a missing name cannot produce 'Hello {user}'. Render here, not in each worker, so email and push stay consistent. Preview in staging is part of safety.

Core concepts in this module

  • Versioned templates
  • Locales
  • Strict variables
  • Preview

3. Channel workers

One worker pool per vendor isolates timeouts. SMS outages should not block push. Workers record provider message IDs. Retries use exponential backoff and a maximum. Permanent errors such as invalid number go to a suppression list. Rate-limit yourself to stay under vendor caps.

Core concepts in this module

  • Per-vendor isolation
  • Backoff
  • Suppression lists
  • Vendor rate caps

4. Preferences and attempt log

Preferences are the user's contract. Attempt logs are yours: what you tried, when, and why it stopped. They power support and compliance. Retention should be long enough to debug and short enough to respect privacy. Do not use the attempt log as a marketing analytics warehouse without a plan.

Core concepts in this module

  • Opt-in / opt-out
  • Audit of sends
  • Retention
  • Support traces

How the modules work together

A service posts an intent: user, template, priority, dedup key. The router checks preferences and quiet hours, renders a template, and enqueues one or more channel jobs. Workers call vendors and record attempts. Temporary failures retry with backoff; permanent failures stop. Security messages use a separate queue so a marketing blast cannot starve them. The original service can poll or subscribe to delivery state if it must.

sections.label: Distributed message queue (Kafka)
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Kafka is a replicated, partitioned commit log. Producers append. Consumers read at their own offsets. Order is per partition, not global. Replication keeps the log alive when a broker dies. Consumer groups divide partitions among workers. Application correctness still depends on what you do when you crash after processing but before committing an offset.

System blueprint

Think 'distributed log,' not 'smart queue that deletes on read.' Retention is time or size, and replay is a feature.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Brokers and partition logs

A topic is split into partitions, each an ordered log on disk. Throughput scales with partitions, but a single key hashes to one partition. Retention lets consumers rewind. Disk layout and page cache are why sequential appends are fast. Choose partition count with future consumers in mind; shrinking is painful.

Core concepts in this module

  • Partitions
  • Append-only logs
  • Retention
  • Key hashing

2. Replication and controller

Each partition has a leader and followers. The in-sync replica set lists who is caught up. Acks=all means the leader waits for ISR. The controller assigns leaders when a broker dies. Replication is not a backup to object storage; it is how the cluster survives a node loss. Unclean leader election is a durability choice you should understand before enabling.

Core concepts in this module

  • Leader / followers
  • ISR
  • Ack modes
  • Controller failover

3. Group coordinator

A consumer group is a team sharing work. The coordinator assigns partitions so each partition has one active reader in the group. Rebalances pause work; cooperative protocols reduce that pause. Static membership helps rolling deploys. This module does not process messages; it decides who may.

Core concepts in this module

  • Consumer groups
  • Rebalance
  • Partition assignment
  • Static membership

4. Offsets

An offset is a bookmark. Commit too early and a crash loses messages. Commit too late and you reprocess. Exactly-once requires transactional producers or idempotent writes in the consumer. Lag is the distance between log end and committed offset; alert on time-to-drain, not only on a raw count.

Core concepts in this module

  • Offset commit
  • At-least-once
  • Idempotent consumers
  • Consumer lag

How the modules work together

A producer chooses a partition, usually by key, and waits for a configured ack. The leader broker appends and followers replicate. The controller manages leadership. Consumers in a group receive a partition assignment from the coordinator and commit offsets as they process. If a consumer dies, partitions rebalance. Hot keys pile onto one partition; that is a design mistake, not a broker bug.

sections.label: Reddit
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Forums generate a storm of tiny writes—votes and comments—and a smaller set of hot read pages. Raw votes should not update a single global counter row on every click. Comments form a tree that cannot be fetched unbounded. Ranking is a projection you can rebuild if the algorithm changes or abuse is reversed.

System blueprint

If you store only the current score, you cannot undo a bot ring. Keep the raw vote.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Post service

Posts belong to a community and have visibility states: live, removed, spam, locked. The listing of a community is not a SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY time. It is a ranked projection. Author edits are versioned so moderation can see what changed. Cross-posts are references, not copies of every comment.

Core concepts in this module

  • Community partition
  • Visibility states
  • Derived listings
  • Edit history

2. Vote aggregator

Each user-post pair should vote at most once (or switch once). Write the raw vote, then update a counter shard. Popular posts need sharded counters or a buffer that flushes. Never lock a single score row for a viral thread. Changing your vote is a new event, not an in-place mystery.

Core concepts in this module

  • Raw vote log
  • Sharded counters
  • One vote per user
  • Async score

3. Comment tree

Comments are a forest. Store parent IDs and maybe a materialized path. Reads request a root plus a depth and a sibling limit. Sort can be new, old, or ranked. Deep threads need lazy load. Deletes become tombstones so children still have a parent to hang from.

Core concepts in this module

  • Adjacency / path trees
  • Depth limits
  • Tombstones
  • Ranked comments

4. Ranker and listing cache

Hot and best are functions of score, time, and sometimes controversy. Compute them in workers and cache community pages. Cache keys must include sort and filters. A removed post invalidates those keys. Rebuild is possible because raw votes still exist.

Core concepts in this module

  • Time-decay ranking
  • Materialized hot lists
  • Cache invalidation
  • Rebuild from events

How the modules work together

A vote writes a raw event and a worker updates a sharded score. Listings read materialized rankings plus a cache. A comment stores a parent ID; the read path returns a depth-limited slice, with 'load more' for the rest. Moderation events flow through the same projections so a removed post disappears from caches. Abuse systems feed the ranker, they do not edit HTML.

sections.label: Pinterest
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Pinterest is a recommendation-heavy graph of users, boards, and pins. The home feed is not only 'people you follow.' It mixes that graph with related content and trends so a new account is not empty. Images are a CDN problem. Relationships and ranking features are a data problem.

System blueprint

Cold start is a first-class module. If the only source is the follow graph, day-one users bounce.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Pin ingest

Ingest stores the image, extracts a signature for near-dup detection, and writes metadata. Scraped URLs need crawler politeness and spam checks. This pipeline is asynchronous so a save feels instant. The pin ID is the join key for graph edges and features.

Core concepts in this module

  • Media ingest
  • Near-dup signatures
  • Spam / crawl rules
  • Async enrichment

2. Graph

Users follow users and boards; pins belong to boards; pins can be related. These edges are candidate fuel. Store them in an access-oriented way: 'pins on this board,' 'followers of this board.' Unfollows and deletes must propagate so a private board does not keep leaking through a cached feed.

Core concepts in this module

  • User/board/pin edges
  • Access-oriented queries
  • Delete propagation
  • Privacy

3. Candidates and ranker

Candidates come from graph neighborhood, visual similarity, and popular topics. Each source should have a quota so one source cannot drown the feed. Ranking uses engagement and freshness. Offline jobs prepare most of this. Online, apply diversity rules so the feed is not twenty near-identical chairs.

Core concepts in this module

  • Multi-source recall
  • Source quotas
  • Diversity
  • Prepared features

4. Image CDN and feature store

Images are resized variants on a CDN. The feature store holds embeddings and counters the ranker needs. Features are versioned because a model trained on last month's schema should not silently read new columns. Evict features for deleted pins.

Core concepts in this module

  • Image variants
  • Feature versions
  • Embedding lookup
  • Deletion hygiene

How the modules work together

A save or upload creates a pin and edges to a board. Ingest extracts image features. Candidate generation reads follows, similar pins, and trends. The ranker orders a bounded set using the feature store. The home feed API pages with a cursor and rechecks that a pin still exists and is allowed. Images never travel through the ranker; the client fetches them from the CDN using keys on the pin.

sections.label: Tinder
sections.html:
What this system is solving

A dating app is geo-aware recommendation plus a tiny set of durable decisions: swipe left, swipe right, and match. Exact GPS should not be a product feature you leak. Candidates are generated in batches, filtered again at serve time, and swipes are append-only so a retry does not create two matches.

System blueprint

The stack you see is a recommendation. The swipe log is the contract. Matches are derived from two complementary likes.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Candidate generation

This module builds a stack using preferences, past swipes, and activity. It should run ahead of the user so swiping feels instant. Exclude already-swiped IDs. For a new user, fall back to popular or recently active profiles in the area. Generation can be approximate; the serve path filters again.

Core concepts in this module

  • Batch stacks
  • Negative filters
  • Cold start
  • Prefetch

2. Geo filter

People are indexed into cells. Query the current cell and neighbors, then widen. Do not return exact coordinates to the other user. Distance bands are enough. Travelers create a burst of writes; those should not explode a single city partition without overflow cells.

Core concepts in this module

  • Cell indexes
  • Neighbor queries
  • Privacy-preserving distance
  • Travel bursts

3. Swipe service

A swipe is unique on (from, to). Replay must not create a second like. Store direction and time. This log is also how you prevent showing the same person again. Rate-limit to reduce bots. The swipe service should not send chat messages; it emits an event if the like might complete a match.

Core concepts in this module

  • Idempotent swipes
  • Uniqueness constraint
  • Replay safety
  • Bot rate limits

4. Match service

A match exists when both sides liked. Create it once, open a conversation, and notify. Unmatching is a state change that should hide history according to policy. This module is small and must be correct; duplicate matches confuse billing and chat authorization.

Core concepts in this module

  • Mutual like
  • Exactly-once match
  • Conversation grant
  • Unmatch policy

How the modules work together

A session asks for a batch. Geo filter keeps people in a coarse radius and preference window. The client swipes. Each swipe is written once. When a like is mutual, match service creates a conversation thread and notifies both sides. Blocks and reports remove people from future batches immediately. Distance is computed from cells, not from a live share of street address.

sections.label: Google Docs
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Collaborative editing is a consistency problem. Two people type in the same paragraph and both expect their words to remain. Operational Transformation (OT) rewrites incoming operations against a server order. CRDTs encode merge rules in the data type so replicas converge. Presence cursors are ephemeral. Version history is a snapshot plus a log you can compact.

System blueprint

Pick a merge rule first. The websocket is just the transport for that rule.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Collaboration socket

This is a sticky session to a document shard so all live editors of a doc meet the same engine. On reconnect the client sends the last operation ID it applied. The socket should not be the database; if it dies, another instance must load the log. Authz is checked here: a viewer cannot submit edits.

Core concepts in this module

  • Sticky sessions
  • Reconnect cursors
  • Document sharding
  • Edit vs view

2. OT / CRDT engine

OT transforms an operation against concurrent ones so the server's order still preserves intent. CRDTs give each insert an identity so replicas can merge without a single transformer. Both need operation IDs and a story for undo. Choose one family and keep it; mixing ad hoc string patches will diverge. Large docs may split into blocks to keep transforms cheap.

Core concepts in this module

  • Operational transformation
  • CRDTs
  • Intent preservation
  • Block sharding

3. Presence

Cursors and selections expire when a socket goes quiet. They are broadcast but not written into the document history. Storing them durably would explode the version list and lie after a laptop sleeps. Color and name are display metadata on the session, not on the paragraph.

Core concepts in this module

  • Ephemeral cursors
  • Session metadata
  • TTL presence
  • No history pollution

4. Snapshotter and version store

The op log grows forever unless you checkpoint. A snapshot is a document state at a sequence. Older ops can be compacted after all clients are beyond them. Named versions are user-facing restore points. Compaction must not destroy legal evidence the product promised to keep.

Core concepts in this module

  • Checkpoints
  • Log compaction
  • Named versions
  • Restore

How the modules work together

An editor connects, loads a snapshot plus recent ops, and sends local operations. The engine assigns a sequence (OT) or merges a CRDT state, then broadcasts to others. Presence pings show cursors. Periodically the snapshotter writes a checkpoint so a new client does not replay years of keystrokes. Comments and suggestions are objects with their own IDs so they can ride the same session without breaking the text merge.

sections.label: Yelp / nearby places
sections.html:
What this system is solving

Nearby search asks: what businesses around this point match a query, and which should appear first? Scanning every restaurant in the country is not an option. Geohashes and quadtrees bucket the map. Ranking then combines distance with review quality. The read path is heavy; writes to hours and reviews are eventually visible.

System blueprint

Cell boundaries miss edge results, so you always search neighbors. Distance alone is a poor ranking function.

Modules in the blueprint

Each box above is a real responsibility. The notes below explain what that module owns, why it exists, and which ideas you should be able to name in an interview or design review.

1. Geo index

Geohash encodes a point into a string prefix that nearby points share. Quadtrees recursively split space where density is high. Either structure turns 'near me' into a few bucket lookups. You must query neighbors because a restaurant across the hash boundary is still next door. Split hot cells; do not keep a single 'downtown' bucket forever.

Core concepts in this module

  • Geohash
  • Quadtrees
  • Neighbor cells
  • Hot-cell splits

2. Ranker

Candidates are cheap; ranking is the product. Signals include distance, rating, review count, category match, and personal history. 'Open now' should be revalidated because hours change. Empty result sets should widen radius or relax filters rather than return a proud zero. Pagination uses a cursor over the ranked list.

Core concepts in this module

  • Distance + quality
  • Open-now recheck
  • Radius widening
  • Cursors

3. Reviews

Reviews are a write-heavy sidecar. They need moderation, spam detection, and an aggregate that can be recomputed. Do not average in place without remembering counts. Photos are objects on a CDN. A review is not a reason to rebuild the entire geo tree.

Core concepts in this module

  • Append reviews
  • Moderation
  • Recomputable aggregates
  • Async document update

4. Business documents and cache

The search document is denormalized: name, coords, category, coarse hours, rating. Details pages can be richer and more cached. When a business moves, both the document and the geo bucket change. Tombestone closed businesses so old deep links explain why a pin vanished.

Core concepts in this module

  • Denormalized docs
  • Details cache
  • Move / rebucket
  • Closed tombstones

How the modules work together

The API receives a point, radius, and text. Geo index returns business IDs in the covering cells plus neighbors. Ranker fetches documents, applies filters such as open-now (rechecked if stale), and sorts. The client then loads details and photos from cache. A new review updates the review store and eventually the document's average; it should not lock the geo index. Hot downtown cells are split so one partition does not own all of a city center.
